newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli unions in wildcat nationwide strike.
newsitem.headline: Israeli unions in wildcat nationwide strike.

text.p: Israeli unions battling privatisation plans launched a nationwide strike on Thursday, grounding summer travellers at Tel Aviv's busy international airport for hours and disrupting rail and postal services.

The Histadrut labour federation said some 60,000 workers at state-owned companies or institutions began an open-ended strike in support of employees of Bezeq Israel Telecom in their fight against a further sell-off of the company.

Tel Aviv's Ben-Gurion international airport, which was particularly hard hit, reopened at 7 p.m. (1600 GMT) after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed to a labour demand he meet union leaders but other state-owned companies stayed shut.

"The prime minister responded to the request of Histadrut secretary-general Amir Peretz and will meet with Histadrut and Bezeq union representatives at 10 p.m. (1900 GMT)," Netanyahu's office said in a statement.
Thousands of summer travellers choked departure halls after the strike grounded planes for 12 hours. Arriving passengers were unable to collect their luggage.
"I hope within a few hours the situation will stabilise," Ben Gurion director-general Avi Kostalitch told Israel radio.

El Al Israel Airlines workers also returned to their jobs but the labour federation said the strike continued at Israel Electric Company, Israeli Military Industries, Israel Aircraft Industries, the Postal Authority, the railroads and other state-owned institutions.
"The Histadrut is dragging the economy towards chaos," Netanyahu's spokesman said earlier in the day.

"The impact is very bad, especially on the economy of the state of Israel," Finance Minister Yaacov Neeman told reporters. Neeman and Communications Minister Limor Livnat were due to join Netanyahu at the meeting with union leaders.
A spokesman for the Israeli Manufacturers' Association said the main damage caused by the strike so far had been "inconvenience".
But he warned that a prolonged walkout could cost the economy up to $30 million a day.

Waiting at Ben-Gurion airport for a flight to Oslo, Ron Nachman, mayor of the Jewish settlement of Ariel in the West Bank, complained: "This is a scandal. It's anarchy. The unions must understand it will boomerang on them."

Haim Katz, head of the workers' committee at Israel Aircraft Industries, said the work stoppage was a warning strike. "We have fired our opening shot, our warning shot. The strike should be as short as possible."

The stoppage was declared hours after the government issued an order to force hundreds of Bezeq employees to restore essential telephone services disrupted in a week-long strike by workers at the country's main telecoms provider.

Union leaders at Bezeq called the move "totalitarian" and said a crisis continued over government plans to privatise more of the state-owned company through the $250 million sale of 12.5 percent of its stock to Merrill Lynch.

Union leaders said the Merrill Lynch deal violated government promises to involve Bezeq workers in all aspects of the company's privatisation and called for the sale to be cancelled or to use its revenues to fund early pension programmes.

"(Thursday's) strike is unnecessary and will not affect the government's intention of opening the economy to competition in various fields while protecting workers' rights," Netanyahu's spokesman said.
